Equivalent air depth.question: What do you know about The equivalent air depth (EAD)?
Equivalent air depth.answer: a way of approximating the decompression requirements of breathing gas mixtures that contain nitrogen and oxygen in diff
Equivalent air depth.fact: The equivalent air depth (EAD) is a way of approximating the decompression requirements of breathing gas mixtures that contain nitrogen and oxygen in different proportions to those in air, called nitrox. The equivalent air depth, for a given nitrox mix and depth, is the depth of a dive when breathing air that would have the same partial pressure of nitrogen.

Equivalent narcotic depth.question: What do you know about Equivalent narcotic depth (END) (historically also equivalent nitrogen depth)?
Equivalent narcotic depth.answer: used in technical diving as a way of estimating the narcotic effect of a breathing gas mixture, such as nitrox, heliox o
Equivalent narcotic depth.fact: Equivalent narcotic depth (END) (historically also equivalent nitrogen depth) is used in technical diving as a way of estimating the narcotic effect of a breathing gas mixture, such as nitrox, heliox or trimix. The equivalent narcotic depth of a breathing gas mix at a particular depth is calculated by finding the depth at which breathing air would have the same total partial pressure of narcotic components as the breathing gas in question.

Fanzor.fact: The Fanzor (Fz) protein is a eukaryotic, RNA-guided DNA endonuclease, which means it is a type of DNA cutting enzyme that uses RNA to target genes of interest. Fanzor belongs to the OMEGA system.

Fanzor.fact: In bacteria, RNA-guided DNA endonuclease systems, such as the CRISPR/Cas system, serve as an immune system to prevent infection by cutting viral genetic material. Fanzor.fact: Evolutionarily, it shares a common ancestor, OMEGA TnpB, with the CRISPR/Cas12 system. Due to the shared ancestry between the OMEGA system and the CRISPR system, the protein structure and DNA cleavage function of Fanzor and Cas12 remain largely conserved.
